5	
6	# Repo map
7	
8	## Goal
9	A reconcile or implement session starts knowing what the workspace is made of, so it spends its turns on the work instead of on discovering the shape of the repo. A mechanical build walks the workspace and records what it finds: the projects and their paths, the folder conventions the tree actually follows, and, per project, an index of its public types and members. The small part — projects and conventions — is given to the session up front; the type index stays on disk and is read when a session needs a signature, so a large repo costs tool calls it would have spent anyway rather than context it cannot afford. Blind planning never sees any of it.
10	
11	## Building the map
12	Run on demand from the command, and by the session start that needs a fresh map.
13	
14	- B1 (docs/features/repo-map.md#Repo map): the command `KiwiAgent: Build Repo Map` writes the map: the workspace's projects — solutions, `.csproj`, `package.json` workspaces — each with its path and kind, and for each project a type index of its public types with their public members, one line each.
15	  - E1: a workspace where no project is recognised still produces a map that states it found none, so the next session start does not rebuild over and over.
16	- B2: the build considers the workspace's source and project files only, skipping generated and ignored locations (`.agent/`, build output, dependency folders, what the workspace ignores); the same set is what "the newest source file" is measured over.
17	- B3 (docs/features/repo-map.md#Repo map): the .NET type index comes from the C# language service when it is available and from a scan of `public` declarations when it is not; the TypeScript index comes from the TypeScript language service. Each project's index states which of the two produced it.
18	  - E2: a language service that is absent, not yet loaded or fails is not a build failure — that project falls back and the build completes.
19	- B4 (docs/features/repo-map.md#Repo map): folder conventions are stated as facts derived from the tree alone, never from any document, and each carries the evidence it rests on ("endpoints live in `src/<Feature>/Endpoint.cs` — 14 of 15").
20	  - E3: a pattern with too few occurrences, or with counterexamples beyond the threshold, is left out entirely rather than stated with a hedge.
21	- B5: the build runs without an engine: no model call, no tokens, no permission prompt.
22	- B6: the build is deterministic — run twice over an unchanged tree it produces byte-identical files, with ordering that does not depend on filesystem enumeration order.
23	- B7: the build replaces its files wholesale and atomically, and two builds asked for at once (two session starts, or the command during a start) resolve to a single build; no reader ever sees a partly written file.
24	
25	## Starting a session that needs the map
26	A reconcile run or an implement session begins, and the map has to be there and current before the first prompt.
27	
28	- B8 (docs/features/repo-map.md#Repo map): a reconcile run and an implement session receive the map's summary as context at their start; a chat session and a plan session do not.
29	  - E4 (docs/intent/agent.md#Phase 1: Blind plan): a plan session cannot reach the map's files at all — its Read and Glob stay scoped to `docs/intent/**` — so blindness holds even if a map exists.
30	- B9 (docs/features/repo-map.md#Repo map): when the map is missing or older than the newest source file, the start builds it first and the session's first prompt is held until the build ends; progress is visible while it runs.
31	  - E5: a build that fails, or exceeds its time bound, does not block the start — the session begins with the previous map if there is one and with none if there is not, and says which.
32	  - E6: a build that finishes while a session is already running does not alter what that session was given; the map a session holds is the one it started with.
33	- B10: the injected summary is size-bounded — the project list, the folder conventions, and per project the path to its type index and the number of public types in it. Where the bound trimmed the list, the summary states how many projects were left out.
34	
35	## Reading a project's types
36	A session that needs an actual signature goes to the index instead of the source.
37	
38	- B11: each project's type index is a file on disk whose path the injected summary names, readable with the session's ordinary read and search tools; it is not size-capped, because it is read on demand and searched, not injected.
39	- B12 (docs/intent/agent.md#Retrieval): the retrieval sub-session reads the same index files with its own tools; nothing about the map is injected into it.
40	- B13: the map's files are generated output, never a session's to edit — the next build rewrites them completely, so an edit made into them does not survive.

1	## A1 (replace) docs/features/repo-map.md#Repo map
2	- from: ruled in the plan session, when the cost of injecting a public type index was weighed
3	- why: intent bounded the map by capping the types it lists, which still puts the whole public surface of a large repo into every session's context and hides what was cut. Splitting it — a small injected summary, the type index on disk and read on demand — keeps the context small without losing the surface.
4	
5	A generated overview of the workspace that reconcile and implement sessions get up front, so they explore less.
6	
7	- Command `KiwiAgent: Build Repo Map` writes the map under `.agent/`; it also runs before a reconcile or implement session starts when the map is older than the newest source file.
8	- Two parts. The summary is what a session is given at start: the project list (solutions, `.csproj`, `package.json` workspaces) with paths, the folder conventions found, and per project the path to its type index and the number of public types in it. The type index is one file per project, public types with their public members, one line each, left on disk.
9	- Only the summary is size-bounded, so it stays a map: a cap on the projects it lists, with a count of what was omitted. A type index is read and searched on demand, so it is not capped.
10	- For .NET the type index comes from the C# language service when available, otherwise from a Roslyn-free scan of `public` declarations; for TypeScript from the TypeScript language service. Each index says which produced it.
11	- The summary is injected as context at session start, not read through tools. The type indexes are read through tools, by the session and by the retrieval sub-session alike.
12	- Chat sessions do not receive the map. Plan sessions cannot reach it: blind planning reads `docs/intent/**` and nothing else.
13	- Folder conventions are stated as facts ("endpoints live in `src/<Feature>/Endpoint.cs`"), derived from the tree with the evidence they rest on, never from the docs.
14	- The map is generated output: the build rewrites it wholesale, no session edits it.
15	
16	Not included: call graphs, cross-project dependency analysis, watching for changes during a session.

1	import { join } from 'node:path'
2	import { ASK_USER_TOOL } from '../openai-session/tools/ask-user'
3	import type { Scope } from './scope-guard'
4	
5	export const DOCS_DIR = 'docs'
6	export const PLAN_DIR = 'plan'
7	
8	export function featureSlug(feature: string): string {
9	  return (
10	    feature
11	      .toLowerCase()
12	      .replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, '-')
13	      .replace(/^-+|-+$/g, '')
14	      .slice(0, 60) || 'feature'
15	  )
16	}
17	
18	export function specPath(cwd: string, feature: string): string {
19	  return join(cwd, PLAN_DIR, `${featureSlug(feature)}.spec.md`)
20	}
21	
22	/** The product's front door counts as intent: what it says it is, not how it is built. */
23	export const README_GLOB = '{README,ReadMe,Readme,readme}.md'
24	
25	/** `ignored` comes from the `kiwiAgent.planIgnore` setting: docs the planner must not see. */
26	export function blindPlanScope(feature: string, ignored: string[] = []): Scope {
27	  const slug = featureSlug(feature)
28	  // The review file holds the human's comments and the planner's resolutions to them.
29	  // The intent file holds amendments to `docs/**` the planner proposes; the human applies them.
30	  const own = [`${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.spec.md`, `${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.review.md`, `${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.intent.md`]
31	  return {
32	    readable: [`${DOCS_DIR}/**`, README_GLOB, ...own],
33	    writable: own,
34	    ignored,
35	  }
36	}
37	
38	/**
39	 * Tools a blind planner gets, by name, on either engine. Edit is for answering
40	 * a comment in place; AskUser is how a gap in intent is settled by the user
41	 * mid-session instead of being written down and waited on.
42	 */
43	export const BLIND_PLAN_TOOLS = ['Read', 'Glob', 'JsonSchema', 'JsonQuery', 'Write', 'Edit', ASK_USER_TOOL]
44	
45	/**
46	 * Phase 1 system prompt. Short on purpose: it states the job and the output
47	 * contract and leaves the reasoning to the model. Direction is proposed in
48	 * chat before any file is written, so the user steers while it is cheap.
49	 */
50	export function blindPlanPrompt(feature: string, cwd: string): string {
51	  const slug = featureSlug(feature)
52	  return `You are planning the feature "${feature}" for a software product, blind to its source code.
53	
54	Why blind: a planner that reads the code inherits the code's mistakes as constraints, and the feature gets shaped to fit the defects. You derive what the feature should do from intent alone, so that a later phase can compare intent with the code and name every disagreement instead of silently absorbing it.
55	
56	What you may read: \`${DOCS_DIR}/**\` (product intent: goals, ubiquitous language, rules, constraints, feature descriptions), the README in the workspace root (what the product is, in its own words) and your own output file. Nothing else exists for you; do not try. Use Glob with path \`${DOCS_DIR}\` to see what is there, then Read what is relevant.
57	
58	Your input: the user's first message describes the feature or user story. Later messages steer, answer your questions or ask for changes.
59	
60	First, direction. In chat, not in a file: the few decisions that shape the feature (what it is, what it is not, where it could go two ways and which way you propose, with the reason) and the questions whose answer would change that. A short message, then stop and wait. Write nothing until the user says go: a full plan in the wrong direction is wasted, so the user steers first.
61	
62	Then, the spec. When the user accepts or adjusts the direction, write one file, \`${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.spec.md\` under ${cwd}, with Write. Structure:
63	
64	\`\`\`markdown
65	---
66	feature: ${feature}
67	status: draft
68	---
69	
70	# ${feature}
71	
72	## Goal
73	One paragraph: who, what, why. Domain language only.
74	
75	## Cancelling an order
76	One line on the situation, when the title is not enough.
77	- B1 (${DOCS_DIR}/intent/orders.md#Cancellation): one observable rule, written so a test can prove it
78	  - E1: situation → expected outcome, an edge of B1
79	- B2: a rule intent is silent on, settled by you as the sensible default
80	
81	## Open questions
82	- Q1: something intent does not settle and only the user can
83	\`\`\`
84	
85	The spec is a contract, and the extension holds you to it on every write:
86	- \`## Goal\` first, as prose. Then one \`##\` section per scenario: a situation from the user's side, named as the user would say it. A small feature has one scenario; a feature is rarely more than four.
87	- A scenario holds behaviours, \`- B1: ...\`, the rules that make up the situation. An edge case, \`  - E1: ...\`, is indented under the behaviour it qualifies: it is a situation that rule has to survive. An edge case that is a rule of its own is a behaviour. Nothing nests deeper.
88	- Behaviours are few and coarse, each one something a single test can prove. There are no invariants, acceptance criteria or task sections: an invariant is a behaviour, an acceptance criterion restates one, and the tests that prove each item are the implementer's evidence, recorded on the tasks later. Anything else is reported back to you as off contract.
89	- Only Goal and one scenario are always there. Open questions exists when there is one, and holds only what is still unanswered: a question the user answered becomes a behaviour or an edge case, not a Q.
90	
91	Rules:
92	- To the point, not complete. An item earns its place only if leaving it out would change what gets built or how it is tested. Do not restate a behaviour as an edge case, do not spec the obvious, do not cover every situation that could be imagined. A feature described in two sentences is usually a page, not five.
93	- No tasks: what to do and where is settled when the spec is mapped against the code, in a file of its own. A task written blind would only restate the behaviours.
94	- Settle what you can. Where intent is silent but a sensible default exists, take it and say so in the direction; a question is for what only the user can answer, and you put it with the \`${ASK_USER_TOOL}\` tool and carry on with the answer rather than writing it down and stopping.
95	- Item ids (B1, E1, Q1) are global and stable: never renumber on revision, never reuse, only add or mark an item removed. Moving an item to another scenario keeps its id.
96	- An item that comes from a section of \`${DOCS_DIR}/**\` cites it in parentheses after the id, as \`path#Heading\`. An item without a citation is your own default. The citation is what a later check against the code reads instead of the docs, so it must be exact.
97	- No code paths, class names or code: that is the implementation's business and you cannot know it. No tables; the Findings table below is not yours.
98	- A \`## Findings\` section may appear in the file, written by a separate check of the spec against the code: a table with the columns Finding and Proposed solution, one row per finding (F1, F2, ...). Each is something the user rules on. When asked, fill in the Proposed solution cell of each open finding with Edit: how the spec should change, or why it should stand as written, with the reason, in one or two sentences. A proposal is not a ruling: change no item until the user has ruled; then revise the items the finding names per the ruling and append \` [resolved]\` to its Finding cell. Leave the Finding column otherwise alone.
99	- When a ruling settles something that \`${DOCS_DIR}/**\` does not say, or says otherwise, record the amendment in \`${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.intent.md\` in the form below. You never edit \`${DOCS_DIR}/\` yourself: intent is the user's, and the user applies these. Record only what outlives this feature — a rule, a term, a constraint — never the feature's own plan.
100	
101	\`\`\`markdown
102	## A1 (append) ${DOCS_DIR}/intent/orders.md#Cancellation
103	- from: F3, ruled for the spec
104	- why: intent does not say what happens to a cancelled order's reservation.
105	
106	Cancelling an order releases its reservation immediately.
107	\`\`\`
108	
109	  The mode is \`append\` (add to the section), \`replace\` (rewrite the section's body) or \`new\` (add a section, or a document that is not there yet). Write the amendment as intent reads: the product's language, present tense, no reference to this spec or its ids. Amendment ids are stable and never reused; leave an applied one alone.
110	- The user reviews the draft by commenting on its items and striking the ones that should not be built; comments, strikes and your answers to them live in \`${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.review.md\`. A submitted review is direction, not a question: revise the spec as it asks, mark every struck item removed without renumbering anything, never bring a struck item back on your own, and answer every comment in that file as addressed or disagreed with a reason.
111	- If ${DOCS_DIR} has nothing on this feature, or the description is too thin to derive a direction, do not invent: ask with \`${ASK_USER_TOOL}\` and work from the answer.
112	- After each write, summarise what changed in a few sentences and stop.`
113	}
114	
115	/**
116	 * The first message of a plan session picked up on a spec another session
117	 * wrote: the files are the state, so the planner reads them and reports where
118	 * the plan stands instead of starting the feature over.
119	 */
120	export function resumePlanPrompt(feature: string): string {
121	  const slug = featureSlug(feature)
122	  return [
123	    `The spec for "${feature}" already exists at \`${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.spec.md\`, written in an earlier session that is gone. Do not start over.`,
124	    '',
125	    `Read it from disk, and \`${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.review.md\` and \`${PLAN_DIR}/${slug}.intent.md\` where they exist. Then, in chat, where the plan stands in a few sentences: its status, open questions, findings without a ruling, comments not yet answered. An approved spec is settled: change nothing in it unless the user asks.`,
126	    '',
127	    'Then stop; the user says what happens next.',
128	  ].join('\n')
129	}
130	
131	/**
132	 * The message the planner gets when a spec is off contract: rearrange, do not
133	 * re-plan. Written for a spec from before the contract as much as for a slip,
134	 * so it says where invariants, acceptance criteria and flat edge cases go.
135	 */
136	export function migrateSpecPrompt(feature: string, problems: string[]): string {
137	  const spec = `${PLAN_DIR}/${featureSlug(feature)}.spec.md`
138	  return [
139	    `The spec for "${feature}" at \`${spec}\` is off contract:`,
140	    ...problems.map((p) => `- ${p}`),
141	    '',
142	    'Read it from disk and rewrite it to the contract with Write, changing the arrangement and nothing else: the rules stay the rules.',
143	    '- Group the behaviours into scenarios, one `##` per situation from the user\'s side; a small feature has one.',
144	    '- Nest every edge case under the behaviour it qualifies, indented as `  - E1: ...`. An edge case that qualifies no single behaviour is a behaviour of its own.',
145	    '- Fold invariants and acceptance criteria into the behaviours they restate; drop what restates without adding. One that is a rule of its own becomes a behaviour with a new B id, and its text ends with `(was I3)` naming the old id, so what referred to it can be renamed.',
146	    '- A `## Tasks` section is deleted: tasks live in the tasks file.',
147	    '- Every B, E, Q and F id that survives keeps its id; Open questions and Findings stay as they are.',
148	    '',
149	    'Then, in chat, one line per item that moved or was folded. Then stop.',
150	  ].join('\n')
151	}

29	export function findings(body: string): Finding[] {

4	export type Scope = {
5	  /** Globs, workspace-relative, of what Read and Glob may see. */
6	  readable: string[]
7	  /** Globs, workspace-relative, of what Write and Edit may touch. */
8	  writable: string[]
9	  /** Globs carved out of `readable`; a match is denied even when readable allows it. */
10	  ignored?: string[]
11	}

13	/**
14	 * Enforces a phase's file scope at the tool call, where the model cannot
15	 * talk its way around it. A blind planner reads intent docs and writes one
16	 * spec; everything else is denied with the reason. A write inside the scope
17	 * is the phase's deliverable, so it goes through without a permission prompt.
18	 */
19	export class ScopeGuard implements SessionHooks {
20	  constructor(
21	    private readonly cwd: string,
22	    private readonly scope: Scope,
23	  ) {}
24	
25	  async preToolUse(tool: ToolUse): Promise<PreToolUseOutcome> {
26	    const input = (typeof tool.input === 'object' && tool.input !== null ? tool.input : {}) as Record<string, unknown>
27	    switch (tool.toolName) {
28	      case 'Read':
29	        return this.check(input['file_path'], this.scope.readable, 'read')
30	      case 'Glob':
31	      case 'Grep':
32	        return this.check(input['path'] ?? '.', this.scope.readable, 'search', true)
33	      case 'Write':
34	      case 'Edit':
35	      case 'MultiEdit':
36	        return this.check(input['file_path'], this.scope.writable, 'write') ?? { allow: true }
37	      case 'NotebookEdit':
38	        return this.check(input['notebook_path'], this.scope.writable, 'write') ?? { allow: true }
39	      case 'Bash':
40	      case 'PowerShell':
41	        return { deny: `${tool.toolName} is not available in this phase.` }
42	      default:
43	        return undefined
44	    }
45	  }
46	
47	  private check(raw: unknown, globs: string[], verb: string, directory = false): PreToolUseOutcome {
48	    if (typeof raw !== 'string') return { deny: `Cannot ${verb}: no path given.` }
49	    const absolute = isAbsolute(raw) ? raw : resolve(this.cwd, raw)
50	    const rel = relative(this.cwd, absolute).split('\\').join('/')
51	    if (rel.startsWith('..')) return { deny: `Cannot ${verb} outside the workspace: ${raw}` }
52	    const ignored = (this.scope.ignored ?? []).find((g) => matchesGlob(rel, g) || (directory && matchesGlob(`${rel}/x`, g)))
53	    if (ignored) return { deny: `Cannot ${verb} ${raw}: excluded from this phase by the ignore setting (${ignored}).` }
54	    // A search directory must itself lie inside the allowed tree: searching
55	    // from the workspace root would list names of files the phase must not see.
56	    const allowed = globs.some((g) => matchesGlob(rel, g) || (directory && matchesGlob(`${rel}/x`, g)))
57	    if (allowed) return undefined
58	    return { deny: `Cannot ${verb} ${raw}: this phase is limited to ${globs.join(', ')}.` }
59	  }
60	}

7	/**
8	 * Where a feature stands, derived from its files under `plan/` and held
9	 * nowhere else: the spec's status, the review, the task board and its
10	 * verification record can never disagree with a stage that is computed from
11	 * them.
12	 */
13	export type PlanStage =
14	  | 'missing'
15	  /** The spec is written; nothing has been said about it. */
16	  | 'created'
17	  /** Comments or strikes are being written, or the planner has yet to answer them. */
18	  | 'under_review'
19	  /** Every comment is answered; the human reads the revised spec and accepts, or comments again. */
20	  | 'final_draft'
21	  /** The spec is mapped against the code: tasks and files exist, work has not started. */
22	  | 'mapped'
23	  | 'under_development'
24	  /** Every task is tested; the test commands have yet to pass. */
25	  | 'verification'
26	  | 'verified'

28	export function planStage(spec: SpecState, review: Review, tasks: TasksState): PlanStage {
29	  if (!spec.exists) return 'missing'
30	  const comments = review.rounds.flatMap((r) => r.comments)
31	  // A review in flight comes first: a re-review after mapping is a review like any other.
32	  if (comments.some((c) => !c.resolution)) return 'under_review'
33	  if (standingStrikes(spec.body, struckItems(review)).length > 0) return 'under_review'
34	  if (comments.some((c) => !c.closed)) return 'final_draft'
35	  if (!tasks.exists) return 'created'
36	  if (spec.status === 'draft' || !started(tasks.tasks)) return 'mapped'
37	  if (!tasksDone(tasks.tasks)) return 'under_development'
38	  return tasks.verification?.ok ? 'verified' : 'verification'
39	}

41	/** The board predates the spec as it stands: a ruling or a revision changed the plan after the tasks were mapped. */
42	export function tasksStale(spec: SpecState, tasks: TasksState): boolean {
43	  if (!spec.exists || !tasks.exists) return false
44	  return !tasksFresh(tasks, specFingerprint(parseSpec(spec.body)))
45	}

48	export const isApprovable = (stage: PlanStage, spec: SpecState, tasks: TasksState): boolean =>
49	  stage === 'mapped' && spec.exists && spec.status === 'draft' && !tasksStale(spec, tasks)

140	## Retrieval
141	
142	A sub-session the planner calls with `retrieve(question, known, budget)` to keep file dumps out of its own context. Phase 2 first; phase 1 only when the intent tree or work-item graph outgrows the planner.
143	
144	- Locates and quotes, never interprets. Output is verbatim excerpts with provenance; the planner rules on them. A summary drops nuance silently, and the planner never sees what was left out.
145	- Tools are derived, not configured: the calling phase's tool set minus AskUserQuestion and anything that writes. Phase 1 retrieval is blind by construction.
146	- No user interaction, no recursion. "Needs X to answer" goes in `not_found`; the planner decides whether to ask. Depth 1.
147	- Result: `findings[]` (excerpt, source as `path#heading`, work item id or URL, one line on why it matches), `not_found[]` (what was looked for, where), `status: complete | partial | budget_exhausted`. Partial is a result, not an error.
148	- Written to `.agent/runs/<id>/retrieval/<n>.md`; the tool returns path, status and counts. Files on disk, not conversation context.
149	- Budget per call (tool calls, tokens), set by the planner. Exhaustion returns findings so far.
150	- Runs as a `CodeSession` under its own profile; a cheap model is fine because the task is search.
151	- Independent questions fan out as independent sessions, no shared state.
152	
153	## Phase 3: Implement
154	
155	Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, JsonSchema, JsonQuery, Bash. Input is the approved spec and its tasks file, fresh session started from the plan bar; refuses to start on `status: draft` or without a tasks file. Breakage findings the user chose to fix are work with the task they touch. Writes go through the ordinary permission prompt; no scope guard.
156	
157	- Task state is the tasks file: the implementer appends `[in progress]` when it starts a task, `[done]` when the code is written, `[tested]` when every item the task delivers is proven by a passing test, `[blocked: reason]` when it cannot finish, so task 4 of 7 survives a fresh session and shows in the plan view. The task's `files:` line is kept true to what was touched.
158	- Coverage is the evidence: a `proves:` line on the task names, per delivered item, the test file and the test whose name states the rule (`proves: B1 test/orders/cancel.test.ts an_open_order_can_be_cancelled, E1 ...`). The plan view shows on each behaviour and edge case which task delivers it and which test proves it, or `no task` / `no test`; a task marked tested with an item it names no test for is flagged. That is what an acceptance section used to promise, made checkable.
159	- Only `[tested]` is a finish. A board whose every task is tested goes to verification; the plan bar stops offering Implement, since a second session would re-read the code and decide for itself what to redo. `[blocked: reason]` is unfinished work, so it still takes a fresh session. The state is derived from the markers, not a `status` of its own: adding a task to a finished board makes it unfinished again with nothing to reset, and the two can never disagree.
160	
161	## Migration
162	
163	`KiwiAgent: Migrate plans` brings every plan under `plan/` to the contract; Repair in the plan bar does it for one. By rule first: a legacy `## Tasks` section becomes the tasks file (delivered ids first, markers kept), the board is stamped, the intent file is parsed and a broken one reported, the review file is untouched. What remains (invariants, acceptance criteria, flat edge cases) goes to the plan session as a prompt: group into scenarios, nest edges, fold restated rules, keep every id, and mark a folded rule that survives under a new id with `(was I3)`. When that turn ends the extension follows each rename through the review targets, the tasks' delivered ids and the findings, drops the notes and stamps the board. Approval is kept on a migrated approved spec: the arrangement changed, not the rules.
164	
165	## Verification
166	
167	Mechanical, no model: once every task is `[tested]`, the extension runs the `kiwiAgent.verify` rules over the files the tasks name. A rule is a file glob, a project marker and a command (`**/*.cs` with `*.csproj` runs `dotnet test` in that project; `src/**/*.ts` with `package.json` runs `npm test` there), so a feature that touched only the backend runs only the backend's tests, and a repo with a backend and a frontend bundle runs each once. The outcome is recorded under `## Verification` in the tasks file, newest first; the output tail goes to the run log. A failure is handed to the implement session (the live one for the feature, or a fresh one) with the command and its output; the run repeats when the board is all tested again, up to `kiwiAgent.verifyFailureBudget` consecutive failures, after which the failed record stays for the user. Verify again is offered from the plan bar.

169	Parked: build scoped to the project owning the edited file; read-before-edit staleness enforced in a hook rather than by prompt.

180	
181	`.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` and `.agent/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, Claude Code's layout, so one skill serves both engines; `.agent/skills` wins on a shared name.
